title: Largest All-Ones Rectangle
statement:
You get a grid grid of characters, each "0" or "1". Think of it as a floor plan where "1" is free space.

Find the largest axis-aligned rectangle that contains only "1" cells and return its area (the number of cells in it). Return 0 if the grid has no "1".

examples.why: Columns 1 to 3 of rows 1 and 2 form a 2 × 3 block. The 2 × 2 block in the top-left corner is smaller.
One row: the answer is the longest run of ones.
The full column on the right has 3 cells, but rows 1–2 across both columns give 4. Tall and thin is not always best.

hints: Fix the bottom row of the rectangle. For each column, how tall a stack of ones stands on that row?
Those heights form a bar chart, and the best rectangle with this bottom row is the largest rectangle under that bar chart.
Update the heights row by row (a 1 adds one, a 0 resets to zero) and solve the bar chart problem each time with a monotonic stack in O(cols).

explain.intuition:
Every rectangle has a bottom row. Fix that row and look up from it: in each column, count how many "1"s stand stacked on top of it without a gap. Those counts are a bar chart, and a rectangle of ones resting on this row is exactly a rectangle under the bar chart. So the 2-D problem becomes the 1-D "largest rectangle in a histogram" problem, once per row.

The heights are cheap to update: moving down one row, a "1" adds one to its column's height and a "0" resets it to zero. The histogram problem is solved with an increasing stack: when a shorter bar arrives, every taller bar on the stack has found its right edge, and the bar below it on the stack is its left edge.
steps: Keep heights, an array of zeros with one entry per column.
For each row: set heights[j] = grid[i][j] === "1" ? heights[j] + 1 : 0.
Run the histogram step on heights: scan columns with a stack of indexes whose heights increase; add a sentinel height 0 at the end.

When the current height is lower than the top's, pop the top t. Its rectangle spans from just after the new top to just before the current column: width j − stackTop − 1 (or j if the stack is empty). Update the best with heights[t] · width.
Return the best area over all rows.
pitfalls: Taking the largest square or the longest run of ones in one row or column; the third example shows a wider, shorter block winning.
Forgetting the sentinel bar at the end of each row, so bars still on the stack are never measured.
Not resetting a column's height to zero on a "0". A rectangle cannot jump across a gap.

solutions.title: Every top-left corner, grow down
solutions.idea: From each cell, extend downward row by row, keeping the narrowest run of ones seen so far as the width.
solutions.time: O(rows² · cols²) in the worst case

solutions.title: Row heights + monotonic stack
solutions.idea: Each row turns the grid above it into a bar chart; solve the largest rectangle in that chart with an increasing stack.

followups: Find the largest square of ones instead. Why does a simple DP beat the stack there?
Count every all-ones rectangle in the grid, not just the largest one.
